artwork_title: A Group of Figures standing by a Column, Two Women, one with a Baby, the other with a Child, and a Man in the Background
material: pen and brown ink and wash, heightened with white gouache on paper
provenance:
Provenance:
Probably the Earl of Arundel
Probably Antonio Maria Zanetti
Thence by descent
Giovanni Antonio Armano (according to the engraved inscription on the related etching by Rosaspina)
T. Philipe (L. 2451)
Sold: Rieunier & Associés, Paris, April 12, 2008, Lot 12
Jean-Luc Baroni, Ltd., London
Acquired from the above by the present owner, 2009

Literature:
A.E. Popham, Catalogue of the Drawings of Parmigianino, New Haven and London, 1971, I, under nos. O.R. 93 and 521, II, pl. 202
Suzanne Folds McCullagh and Laura M. Giles, Italian Drawings before 1600 in the Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago, 1997, no. 217, pp. 168-169

Lot Essay:
Until recently, this drawing was known only through an etching by Francesco Rosaspina (c. 1762-1841), part of a set of facsimiles after Parmigianino acquired by the British Museum in 1919. Eight etchings in the group, including this one, bear inscriptions indicating they reproduced works from the collection of Giovanni Antonio Armano, a late 18th century Venetian dealer. The Rosaspina print, in reverse to the actual drawing and showing slightly more of the right-hand figure, led scholar A.E. Popham to assert it depicted a genuine Parmigianino work from his Roman period.

Popham connected the drawing to Parmigianino’s Marriage of the Virgin in the École des Beaux-Arts, and to other pen-and-wash compositions with looping lines and atmospheric effects. These include the Pool of Bethesda in a private collection, Christ Healing the Sick (Musée des Beaux-Arts, Angers), and The Worship of Jupiter (British Museum). All are thought to be influenced by Raphael’s Vatican frescoes, particularly The School of Athens, and his tapestry designs for the Sistine Chapel.

The present drawing's dramatic light effects, enhanced with white heightening, suggest a nocturnal scene illuminated from within a nearby building—possibly a temple. One central figure gestures forward while looking back, hinting at a broader narrative or crowd, as seen in related works.

Popham’s belief that this piece was part of a larger composition is supported by parallels with the Art Institute of Chicago drawing, once also known only through prints. Both reflect Parmigianino’s imaginative engagement with Raphael’s elegant style during this lesser-understood, experimental phase of his career.

artwork_title: St. John the Evangelist
material: oil on canvas
provenance:
Dr. Sandro Bellesi has previously confirmed in 2017 the attribution of the present work on the basis of photographs.

Provenance:
Jean-Luc Baroni, Ltd., London
Acquired from the above by the present owner

Literature:
Sandro Bellesi, Pittura e Scultura a Firenze (Secoli XVI-XIX), Florence, 2017, pp. 12-14, fig. 9, illus.

Lot Essay:
Cesare Dandini, a prominent Florentine painter of the 17th century, trained under Francesco Curradi, Cristofano Allori, and Domenico Cresti (Il Passignano). By 1621, he had established himself as an independent artist and quickly gained prestigious patrons, including Prince Don Lorenzo de’ Medici and Grand Duke Ferdinando II. Dandini became known for refined half-length allegorical and biblical figures, marked by rich color, graceful poses, and polished execution.

This painting of Saint John the Evangelist exemplifies Dandini’s mature style. The young saint, set against a plain background, is shown sharpening his quill while his Gospel lies open. His traditional symbol, the eagle, rests before him holding a large book. The cool tones of John’s skin and the vibrant sheen of his satin garments reflect Dandini’s fully developed technique and training.

A nearly identical version of this composition exists in the Guido Bruscoli collection in Florence. Dr. Sandro Bellesi dates that painting to the early 1630s and suggests the present work was completed later, with more refinement in the face and drapery. This painting may have been intended as part of a series of the Four Evangelists, a subject Dandini explored more than once during his career.

artwork_title: The Head of a Man in Profile, Looking Up
material: pen and brown ink and brown wash
provenance:
Provenance:
The family of the Artist's nephews Benedetto and Cesare Gennari, Bologna, until c. 1719 (their inscription 10 P. ' Dol.)
Francesco Forni, Bologna
John Bouverie (died 1750)

Bequeathed to Sir Charles Middleton, later 1st Baron Barham (died 1813)

Sold: Sotheby's, London, May 22, 1928, Lot 60
John Nicholas Brown, Providence, Rhode Island, by 1930
David Tunick Inc., New York, 1986
Jeffrey E. Horvitz Collection, Boston, by 1991
Sold: Sotheby's, New York, January 23, 2008, Lot 50

Exhibited:
London, Burlington Fine Arts Club, May-July, 1923, pl. 52, illus.
London, Magnasco Society, Catalogue of a Loan Exhibition of Drawings, XVII-XVIII Century, 1927, no. 6
London, Royal Academy, Italian Art: 1200-1900, January-March, 1930, no. 651a
Gainesville, Florida, University of Florida, Samuel P. Harn Museum of Art, Italian Old Master Drawings from the Collection of Jeffrey E. Horvitz, July 12 - September 8, 1991, no. 20, pp. 80-83, (and traveling) (as Head of a Monk, Possibly St. Francis)

Literature:
A.G.B. Russell, Drawing by Guercino, London, 1923, pp. 20-21; 58, pl. XVII, illus. (as Profile of a Monk)
T. Borenius (anonymously), "Drawing in the Collection of Mr. Archibald G.B. Russell," The Connoisseur, vol. LXVI, May 1923, pp. 3-12, pl. V, illus.
H. Tietze, European Master Drawings in the United States, New York, 1947, no. 56, p. 112, illus. (Profile Head of a Monk)
Sir Denis Mahon, I disegni del Guercino della collezione Mahon, Bologna, 1967, p. 18, note 49
D.M. Stone, Guercino, Master Draftsman: Works from North American Collections, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1991, no. 182, pp. 223; 233, pl. E, illus.

Lot Essay:
The present lot was once part of the large group of drawings which, on Guercino's death, were inherited by his nephews Benedetto (1633-1715) and Cesare (1637-1688) Gennari. By the middle of the eighteenth century, the drawings passed to Cesare's grandson, Carlo Gennari (1712-1790), by whom the group was dispersed. At this point, many drawings, including this sheet, were obtained by the Bolognese dealer, Francesco Forni, who then sold them to John Bouverie. (N. Turner and C. Plazzotta, Drawings by Guercino from British Collections, exhibition catalogue, London 1991, p. 8) According to an inventory of the Gennari family's property taken in 1719, prior to the dispersal of the drawings, 1,689 of them were placed in eight large albums, which were organized according to the medium and subject of the drawing. (D. Mahon and N. Turner, The Drawings of Guercino in the Collection of her Majesty the Queen at Windsor Castle, Cambridge 1989, pp.xx-xxi) One of these albums was entitled Dissegni di Penna, et Acquarella di diverse grandezze, rapresentanti diverse Teste, Figure, e Puttini; it contained 297 drawings, of which the present study was most probably one. (See Gainesville, et al., 1991-93, loc. cit.)

In Linda Wolk-Simon's entry on this drawing in the catalogue of the 1991-3 Horvitz Collection exhibition, she suggested that it has certain affinities with the kneeling St. Francis in Guercino's altarpiece of 1639-41, which depicts the Madonna and Child with Ss. Francis and Clare (Parma, Galleria Nazionale). (See D.M. Stone, Guercino: Catalogo completo dei dipinti, Florence 1991, cat. no. 165)  However, since the exhibition catalogue was published, an altarpiece by Guercino has come to light that may provide a stronger connection. The pala in question, which was documented but thought to have been lost, dates from 1663, and depicts the Madonna and Child appearing to Beato Marcolino Ammani di Forlí: it is to the latter figure that the present study appears to relate. The painting was discovered by Prisco Bagni, badly damaged and in storage at the Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan. It was subsequently cleaned, restored, and published by Bagni in 1991 as a late work, dating from 1663. Before the discovery of the painting, the composition was known, but only from a 1757 engraving by Bolzoni. (D. Mahon, P. Bagni et al, Giovanni Francesco Barbieri, il Guercino, 1591-1666, exh. cat., Bologna 1991, cat. no. 152; the engraving reproduced in P. Bagni's note on the painting in M. Foschi and G. Viroli (eds.), Il San Domenico di Forlí. La chiesa, il luogo, la città, exh. cat., Forlí, Oratorio di San Sebasiano, 1991, pp. 98, 101) Bagni also identified another drawing connected with the painting, a double-sided red chalk sheet, also in the Brera, which has a compositional study on the recto and a study for the kneeling friar on the verso. (P. Bagni in Il San Domenico di Forli, exh. cat., op. cit., pp. 99-100)

The present sheet is drawn in a notably different manner from the red chalk drawing, with broad, bold pen and brown ink, and wash, rather than the more tentative, loosely sculpted chalk of the double-sided study, which fits with what Nicholas Turner describes as the 'broken contours and lines of fluctuating intensity' of Guercino's late period. (Turner and Plazzotta, op.cit., p. 181) As Turner has also pointed out, the present study, on the other hand, can best be related stylistically to Guercino's drawings of the 1630s, and in particular to certain drawings of half- or bust-length single male figures that he made at this time, such as the Old Bearded Man (Royal Library, Windsor Castle), the Man Reading at a Table (Fogg Art Museum, Cambridge, Massachusetts), and the Bust of a Man, facing right (Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York). (Turner's observations cited by Wolk-Simon in the 1991-3 Horvitz exhibition catalogue, loc. cit.)

This difference in style between the two sheets may confirm Wolk-Simon's hypothesis that the present drawing was not drawn in preparation for a painting, but was instead an 'independent invention,' which accounts for the study's highly poetic nature, and the wonderfully broad, fluid manner in which it has been drawn. Indeed, considering it is thought that Guercino drew far less in the 1650s and 60s, and that his doctor had apparently forbidden him from drawing on account of chest pains, the idea that the artist might have used an earlier design, from one of his most intensive periods of draftsmanship, as inspiration for his last painting seems both appealing and plausible. (Turner and Plazzotta, op. cit., p.181)

auction_title: Sale 6343 - Echoes of the Past: Property from an Important Private Collection
artwork_title: Mary Magdalene
material: oil on canvas
provenance:
Dott. Riccardo Lattuada has previously confirmed the attribution of the present work, dating it to the 1740s and noting that it is one of the best extant versions of the composition by the artist.

Provenance:
Private Collection, Spain
Jean-Luc Baroni, Ltd., London, 2011
Private Collection
Sold: Christie's, New York, April 27, 2017, Lot 44

Lot Essay:
In 1503, following the defeat of French forces at the Battle of Garigliano, Spain took control of the city of Naples, establishing it as an important center of their empire. This occupation created opportunities for painters living and working in the city to expand their markets and for increased artistic exchange between Italy and Spain.

One of the most successful artists in Naples to profit from the Spanish rule during the mid-17th century was Andrea Vaccaro. By the 1630s, Vaccaro, a native of the city, had become one of its leading painters, working frequently for Spanish patrons and regularly exporting his work to the Iberian Peninsula (as a result, the Museo del Prado in Madrid has a significant collection of his works). His paintings graced all of the major local collections of the day, including that of the Viceroy of Naples, Gaspar de Bracamonte (c. 1595-1676).

Vaccaro was drawn early on to the dramatic chiaroscuro of Caravaggio, whose Flagellation he copied (Museo di Capodimonte, Naples). The present Magdalene elegantly combines the drama and color of Naples and Rome with the restrained classicism of Guido Reni and Domenichino, who strongly influenced Vaccaro from around 1630, as seen in the Magdalene’s delicate, porcelain features and lyrical pose and expression. The stark tenebrism of the Spanish painter Jusepe de Ribera, who had moved to Naples in 1616, is also particularly evident in the present painting, in the still life at lower left and the somber simplicity of the background.

The evident popularity of the Magdalene as a subject during this period is attested to by the number of paintings Vaccaro produced of the saint. Vacarro's paintings of female figures for his Neapolitan patrons, usually on a more profane theme, were much demanded and have been described as presenting a female ideal combining latent sensuality with a classically derived composure. This figure of Mary Magdalen, as befits her historical character, occupies the territory between sensuousness and piety.

There are several autograph and studio versions of this composition, of varying quality, including paintings in the Museo del Capodimonte, Naples; the Galleria Nazionale di Palazzo Abatellis, Palermo; the State Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg; the Palacio de Liria, Madrid; the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, Rio de Janiero; and the Alte Pinakothek, Munich. The present canvas and one in a private collection in Naples are the only two to bear Vaccaro’s distinctively elegant monogram. Additionally, as Riccardo Lattuada has noted, with its qualities of refinement and noticeable delicacy, both in the execution and characterization of the saint, the present painting is one of the best extant versions.

artwork_title: The Holy Family with God the Father and the Holy Spirit above: a Sacra Conversazione
material: oil on copper
provenance:
Francesca Baldessari previously assisted with cataloguing the present lot, which is now included in her catalogue raisonné on the artist.

Provenance:
Possibly mentioned in the 1727 inventory of Gian Gualberto Guicciardini (inherited by his son-in-law Marchese Rinuccini the following year, as sacra conversazione in figure intere piccole, con cornice intagliata e dorata di Carlino Dolci)
Antinori Family Collection, Italy
Sold: Sotheby's, New York, January 27, 2005, Lot 153
Jean-Luc Baroni Ltd., London
Acquired from the above by the present owner, 2006

Literature:
Francesca Baldessari, Carlo Dolci: Complete Catalogue of the Paintings, Florence, 2015, no. 11, pp. 88-89, illus.

Lot Essay:
This exquisitely finished small copper, unpublished until now, dates to around 1630 and marks a significant early work by Carlo Dolci. Created when the artist was still a teenager, it reflects the formative influence of his master, Jacopo Vignali. Early paintings by Dolci are extremely rare, making the rediscovery of this piece an important addition to his oeuvre.

The subject is an unusual variation on the Sacra Conversazione, a long-standing Florentine theme. Here, the mature Christ is positioned between the Virgin and Saint Joseph, with the Holy Spirit above and God the Father above that, uniting both the Terrestrial and Celestial Trinities in a single composition. This highly theological interpretation reflects the intellectual seriousness that would define Dolci’s career, even at such a young age.

Stylistically, the painting relates closely to Dolci’s early works, such as The Adoration of the Shepherds (formerly Wengraf, Ltd., and Burghley House), with similar facial types, strong overhead lighting, and a restrained palette. Baldessari notes direct borrowings from Vignali’s Baptism of Christ (1627, Villa Strozzi), particularly in the figure of God the Father, setting a post-1627 date for the work. Influences from Matteo Rosselli are also seen in the simplicity of the composition and the Virgin’s delicate profile.

The painting may be identified with a sacra conversazione listed in the 1727 inventory of Gian Gualberto Guicciardini and later in the Antinori collection, both of whom owned works by Dolci (see Baldassari, Carlo Dolci, 1995, pp. 33–34, 168–169, 197).

artwork_title: The Head of a Bearded Man Looking Down
material: oil on canvas
provenance:
Annalisa Scarpa Sonino has previously confirmed the attribution of the present lot to Ricci.

Provenance:
Private Collection, France
Jean-Luc Baroni, Ltd., London, 2014, cat. no. 8

Lot Essay:
Exceptionally refined amongst Ricci's surviving head studies, this beautifully painted and powerful work has been dated by Annalisa Scarpa Sonino to the late 1690s. Although the handling is typical of Ricci, the painting is rather unique amongst his identified works. A well-known series of head studies from the Consul Smith collection, purchased by George III and now at Hampton Court, all record figures from Veronese's painting now in the Gallerie dell' Accademia, The Feast in the House of Levi. Apart from these, an imposing self-portrait painted for the collection of the Medici Grand Dukes and an elegant, classicized profile study of a woman appear to be the only other works by Ricci done in a portrait format.

Dignified and profoundly thoughtful, the present figure is swathed in a blue coat with a brown silk stripe, the style of which is strongly reminiscent of the robes worn by Veronese's sitters. The long beard also gives the man a senatorial air, but his hair is tousled, creating an informal effect. It is tempting to believe that the work is a portrait of a fellow artist, friend, or relation. As a prototype, with its rich painterliness and strong contrasts of light and shade, the painting prefigures the splendid series of philosophers and Orientalists painted by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, and his son and nephew.

artwork_title: The Flight into Egypt
material: pen and brown ink and watercolour over traces of black chalk
provenance:
Dr. Mary Newcome Schleier has previously confirmed the attribution, suggesting that stylistically this drawing appears to be a late work.

Provenance:
Property of Giancarlo Baroni, Switzerland
His posthumous sale, Sotheby's, New York, January 29, 2013, Lot 92

Lot Essay:
In the second half of the 17th century, Domenico Piola can be counted among the most important and influential artists active in Genoa. He was the leading member of a local artistic dynasty, and one of the most sought-after decorative fresco painters in the city, who worked on the large-scale fresco decoration of numerous churches, palaces and villas. The peak of the artist's activity as a frescante was the 1670s and 1680s, which culminated in such works as the extensive decoration of the church of San Luca and the allegorical ceiling frescoes of Autumn and Winter in the Palazzo Rosso. Relatively few paintings from this part of the artist's career survive, however, due to the French bombardment of Genoa that led to the destruction of much of his work in various churches and palaces in the city.

Piola’s facility as a draftsman can be seen in the present drawing. In it, the Christ Child is held protectively by a veiled and youthful Madonna surrounded by angels and putti. The composition is drawn entirely in brown ink, and alternates between thin sharp detail with soft shading that contrasts with the thicker, flowing lines delineating the figures. This line and shading heightens the dynamism and movement, and the addition of watercolor, which is extremely rare in the artist's preparatory studies, adds charm and vibrancy to the scene.

artwork_title: A Figure Tied to a Tree discovered by a Man Walking
material: pen and brown ink and wash
provenance:
Michael Mahoney, author of The Drawings of Salvator Rosa, 1977, has previously confirmed the present work is likely an early drawing.

Provenance:
Dutch Private Collection, probably bought at auction
Paul Brandt, sale, Amsterdam, date unknown (bears pencil inscription on accompanying paper folder: S. Rosa/ Brandt btz 22 f110,-/ No 449i

Lot Essay:
Originally from Naples, where he first trained as an artist, Salvator Rosa moved to Rome in 1635. He joined the household of Cardinal Francesco Maria Brancaccio, a well-connected Neapolitan with literary and intellectual tastes. Rosa’s own poetic and theatrical talents attracted many patrons and supporters, and his friends and fellow artists delighted in his inventive, witty, and often outrageous conversation. Despite this seemingly light deportment, however, there was a disillusionment and darkness, partly connected to the uncertainty and violence in Neapolitan society and politics, but also indicative of his occasionally misanthropic character.

In 1639, Rosa made a series of landscape paintings peopled with ruffians and travelers, in part inspired by the work of the Bamboccianti painters, the rambunctious group of Dutch artists who lived nearby. As Michael Mahoney has kindly confirmed, the present work must be an early drawing, particularly Riberesque and
exceptional for being a fully realized composition from a period when most of Rosa’s surviving work is sketchy and fragmentary. The subject is particularly poignant, in light of the uncertain and dangerous society in which Rosa lived, and his habit of wandering the Naples countryside to sketch. A simply dressed man, perhaps robbed of his outer garments, is bound outstretched along the branches of a half-dead tree. A passerby points to the figure. The unusual event is particularly emphasized by the otherwise undisturbed landscape, with a sunlit plain and town in the distance. The elegant draftsmanship and the application of the wash in to convey the dappled light on the tree trunk and leaves, but an absence of any shading on the trousers of the hanging figure, adds starkness to the strange scene.

material: red chalk
provenance:
Provenance:

Lot Essay:
Baldassare Franceschini, known as Volterrano, was a preeminent fresco painting in Florence in the latter half of the 17th century. His first significant independent commission came in 1636, when he was entrusted by Don Lorenzo de' Medici with the fresco decoration of the courtyard of the villa of La Petraia, near Florence. Volterrano also painted frescoes and altarpieces for numerous churches and palaces in Florence, Volterra, and Rome. His large-scale, crowded fresco compositions reflect an adaptation into a Florentine idiom of the Roman Baroque style, derived from Pietro da Cortona's frescoes in the Palazzo Pitti. His work culminated in the cupola fresco of The Coronation of the Virgin. Commissioned by the Grand Duke Cosimo III, the fresco was the artist's last major project, as he suffered a stroke shortly after its completion.

The present work is a preparatory drawing for one of the lunettes of the chapel dedicated to Saint Auxanus (San Ansano) in the Church of the Sanissima Annunziata in Florence. The chapel was decorated in 1643, on the commission of Giovanni Grassi, who was a well-known musician in his youth. It shows the present cello-playing angel seated at the center of the composition. Another preparatory study includes a brisk and energetic sketch for the whole lunette that shows this angel flanked by two others (Castello Sforzesco, Milan), as well as an impressive and finished modello for the lunette in the Musée Bonnat-Helleu at Bayonne.

Literature:

Lot Essay:
Alessandro Magnasco received his artistic training in Milan, where he spent much of his early career as a specialist in figure painting, often hired to depict staffage in the landscape and architectural paintings of other artists. However, it was only in the 1720s, when he was in his 50s, that the artist began to produce his own independent landscape paintings. These works are distinctive, characterized by rapid flickering brushwork, sepulchral lighting, and curiously dissolved, almost liquified forms, and often peopled with beggars, vagabonds, hermits, saints, monks, and torturers. Such figure types are indicative of the influence of the 17th century Dutch and Flemish genre paintings, which the artist would have seen in the collections of the Medici court in Florence while in their employ.

Only a relatively few compositional drawings by Magnasco are known today. Many of the extant drawings are studies of individual figures or small groups of figures, meant to be inserted into larger painted compositions. The present sheet relates to a bozzetto of the Nativity, now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art (inv. 50-4-11). In both, the composition is almost identical; the figure of Joseph emerges from the shadows, his knees bent, back arched, and gnarled hands gripping a staff. His pose leads to the central scene of Mary, her elegantly elongated features drawn in profile, gazing down at the baby Jesus. In each, intensely dramatic contrasts of light and dark define shape and form, with the actively applied brushwork recalling the energetic, flickering strokes and resplendent impasto of the artist's oil paintings.

This bozzetti is one of a series of four, previously in the Ildebrando Bossi Collection, Genoa. The three other bozzetti represent The Flight into Egypt (Cleveland, Museum of Art, inv. 48.13), The Visitation (present location unknown) and The Mystic Marriage of Saint Catherine (Kansas City, Nelson-Atkins Museum, inv. 47-93).

artwork_title: Lucius Junius condemning to death his sons Titus and Tiberius & A Compositional study
material: black chalk, pen and black ink, grey wash (recto); black chalk (verso)
provenance:
Provenance:
Sold: Christie's, London, July 5, 2011, Lot 93

Lot Essay:
In 1807, Bartolomeo Pinelli was 26 years old and, after training in the studio of Felice Giani, had set up a studio of his own. At this date, the artist was involved in a number of different projects. He worked closely with Franz Kaisermann, painting staffage in some of his landscapes, and he was beginning to work on his famous prints of Roman costume, the first collection of which (Costumi romani) was published in 1809, with another (La nuova raccolta di cinquanta motivi pittoreschi e costumi di Roma) published the following year. The present drawing and the prior lot clearly demonstrate that he was also absorbed with scenes from Classical literature and history, which would later come to fruition in illustrations for the Aenied (1811) and on the subject of Greek history (1812).

Lucius Junius Brutus has traditionally been seen as the founder of the roman Republic, owing to his part in the expulsion of the Tarquin Kings of Rome. The present drawing shows the event which confirmed Brutus as a role model for Roman stoicism: as Consul, he uncovered a plot to return the Tarquins to the throne. His own two sons were implicated and, rather than cheapen the justice of the Republic, Brutus condemned them to dealt as traitors along with the others involved. He then watched the sentence carried out upon them, to emphasize his commitment to the new regime.

The subject of Brutus condemning his sons had particular resonance for Pinelli, as it was the subject of a bas-relief he had submitted to the Accademia Clementina in Bologna in 1798, during his family's exile there. Pinelli was granted the prize for his work, which was his first taste of critical acclaim. He used the present work, with some changes to the composition, as the basis for one of the engravings in his Istoria romana, inventata ed incisa da Bartolomeo Pinelli romano, published in Rome in 1821.

artwork_title: The Head of a Woman Looking to her Left
material: pastel on paper
provenance:
Provenance:
Sold: Chartres, Lelièvre, Maiche, Paris, October 24, 1999, Lot 182 (as 'Attributed to Rosalba Carriera')
Jean-Luc Baroni, Ltd., London
Private Collection
Sold, New York, Sotheby's, January 31, 2018, Lot 164

Literature:
N. Jeffares, Dictionary of pastellists before 1800, online edition, no. J.9.5817 (under 'Anonymous French School')

Lot Essay:
Unique within Le Moyne’s known oeuvre, the present pastel depicts an attractive young woman, her head turned to the right and in a loose chemise. It is a compelling addition to the very few pastels by the artist that survive today.

François Le Moyne, pupil of Louis Galloche (1670-1761), won the coveted Prix de Rome in 1711 but was not offered the traditional trip to Rome due to the economic climate in France at the time. Le Moyne only travelled to Italy in the early 1720s and stayed for a few short months. While there he was greatly influenced by Italian artists such as Correggio and Pietro da Cortona, and the Sienese painter Federico Barocci. 

Elected professor of the Académie de Peinture in 1733, Le Moyne's pupils included Charles Joseph Natoire and François Boucher. Le Moyne was held in high regard during his lifetime and produced magnificent ceiling decorations at Versailles, including for the famous Salond'Hercule. His drawings were collected by the most discerning connoisseurs of the century.

Throughout his short career, Le Moyne used three basic techniques when working on his drawings. His methods are concisely documented by Jean-Luc Bordeaux, in his 1984 monograph on the artist, as red chalk drawings on beige paper; black chalk studies heightened with white chalk on blue or grey paper; and finally trois crayons and/or pastels. (Jean-Luc Bordeaux, François Le Moyne and his Generation, 1688-1737, Neuilly-sur-Seine, 1984, p. 139) Bordeaux highlights the fact that works in both trois crayons and pastel are rare but remarks that Donat, one of Le Moyne’s first biographers, "reported that Le Moyne took great pains in making specific pastel studies of heads of the principal figures in his most important commissions…" (Ibid.) This revealing comment suggests that this was an important element in Le Moyne’s artistic endeavors, despite very few surviving pastels.

In a communication to a previous owner, Jean Luc Bordeaux supports the attribution of the present pastel to Le Moyne. While the head study does not relate directly to any known painting, Bordeaux identifies a number of painted figures by the artist to which she can be plausibly compared, on the basis of the facial type and tilt of the figure's head, as well as a variety of other nuances. He likens this beautiful head to the maiden in A maiden soaking a small piece of cloth in a fountain (known in two versions, in private collections), in which the facial features are similarly rendered in terms of the eyes and lips, and the manner in which the artist has handled the hair and ribbon is also comparable. Bordeaux also cites the figure of Andromeda in the Perseus and Andromeda in the Wallace Collection, where again facial features such as the chin and almond shaped eyes are very comparable, and the Venus in Venus and Adonis in the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm, in which once more the nose and lips, and handling of the hair, are all very similar.

Other stylistic elements identified by Bordeaux as typical of the artist's work include the rapid, rounded strokes made with a hard pastel stick to define the hair, and the light stumping around the corners of the figure's mouth, eyebrows, and eyelids. Also noted by Bordeaux is Le Moyne's overall preference for the consistency of softer pastel sticks and colors, often blended with cloth or brush, to convey the luminosity and smooth uninterrupted tonal textures of the sitter's skin. This softness is emphasized by the artist's more sculptural and angular treatment of the border of her negligée and the lively hair tendrils curling over the sitter's neck and along her shoulders. stands out against the more angular lines used to describe the borders of her garment. It is difficult to find close comparisons to the present pastel and others by the artist, as almost all of Le Moyne's known works in pastel or colored chalks are representations of men.

Le Moyne’s close relationship with his patron and friend François Berger has led Bordeaux tentatively to suggest that this beguiling and beautiful young woman may have been a member of the social circle of Berger and his wife. Her identity is, however, irrelevant to our appreciation of this refined image, or to the light that it sheds on our understanding of Le Moyne's work in this medium, a fascinating aspect of the artist's short but fruitful career.

provenance:
Provenance:

Lot Essay:
Born in Geneva, Ferrière probably received his early training with Jean-Étienne Liotard before moving to Paris to study at the Académie des Beaux-Arts under Joseph-Marie Vien. By 1770, he had returned to his native city where he established himself as a painter and is documented ‘restoring’ paintings belonging to the city’s library. With the outbreak of the French Revolution and the ensuing unrest in Switzerland, Ferrière and his family emigrated to England, where the painter began specializing in miniatures. His portraits were successfully received in London, and he obtained commissions from members of the aristocracy and the Royal Family, and became a frequent exhibitor at the Royal Academy from 1793. After a period in Russia, the artist spent some time working in London before returning to Switzerland, where he once again became a prominent artistic figure and member of the Société des Arts.

This lively depiction of a young boy carrying a painting under his arm is a rare example for a painter that is best-known as a miniaturist. It demonstrates Ferrière's exceptional clarity and refinement of technique in oil, while at the same time bringing light and character to the portrayal. Comparable in tone and composition to pictures Ferrière would likely have seen in Paris, like Vien’s Portrait of Jacques-Louis David as a youth, c. 1765 (Angers, Musée des Beaux-Arts), the present portrait shows a remarkable sense of vivacious naturalism. The young boy's face is animated by the glinting reflections in his eyes, the deep shadow cast by the bucket hat, as well as as his ruddy cheeks and upturned mouth. With the frame tucked under his arm and one finger pointing, the appears poised for movement, as if just sent off on an errand.

Lot Essay:
In addition to his celebrated portraits of famous sitters such as Giuseppe Verdi, James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Consuelo Vanderbilt, the Duchess of Marlborough, and Count Robert de Montesquiou, in the mid-1880s Giovanni Boldini, began to turn to daily objects for inspiration. In these watercolors, scattered paint brushes, plaster busts, vases of flowers and pieces of furniture from his studio repeatedly appear, with the artist exploring their aesthetic possibilities.

In the present work, the arrangement is casual and artful, dominated by the overturned sugar bowl (which also appears in his The Corner of the Painter’s Table, c. 1897, Museo Boldini, Ferrara) and porcelain basket filled with shiny cherries. The repeated, curvilinear forms enhance the tactility of the subject, with movement given by the single spilled cherry cropped at the center right edge. The artist captures the precise details of the still life with broad strokes of watercolor and leaves areas of the white paper exposed to create the gleam of the silver sugar bowl and slatted design of the basket. Every element demonstrates the artist's brilliant confidence with the medium.

artwork_title: Young Woman with a Bouquet of Flowers
material: pastel on paper
provenance:
The Boldini-De Nittis-Zandomeneghi Archives has previously confirmed the authenticity of this lot, which is referenced under Archiving Certificate n. 418673 issued on December 18, 2017. This certificate is now lost.

Provenance:
Durand-Ruel, Paris (possibly his label on the verso:?277 / Zandomeneghi / [jeu]ne femme au / bouquet des fleurs / 267 ...- pastel),
acquired directly from the Artist
Sold: Sotheby's, New York, January 31, 2018, Lot 217

Lot Essay:
This striking work exemplifies Zandomeneghi’s skill with the delicate medium of pastel. The artist adopted in the 1890s, mainly using it for his portraits of women and children. Like many of his favorite subjects, Young Woman with a Bouquet of Flowers depicts the late nineteenth century life of the Parisienne. However, while fellow Italian expatriates like Giuseppe de Nittis and Giovanni Boldini favored painting fashionably dressed ladies, Zandomeneghi preferred portraying women and girls observed in the private moments of their everyday life. 

In the present work, the cropping of the composition and slight lean of the figure’s posture creates a sense of intimacy and connects subject and viewer. The artist suggests the softness of his model’s pale skin with the pastel, and leaves the exposed paper to create highlights along her forehead and cheek. A rich buildup of the medium creates thick, soft upswept strands of hair decorated with a finely carved wooden hairpin, perhaps an allusion to the contemporary trend of Japonisme­. Zandomeneghi’s subtly shifts the soft pinks and buttery yellows of casually arranged daisies with the vibrant blue of cornflowers, while white swirls and wavy vertical lines create abstract patterns of fabric and wallpaper. The complex intertwining of tone and texture is a hallmark of the artist’s best pastels.

A Venetian by birth, Federico Zandomeneghi associated with the Macchiaioli in Florence before moving to Paris in 1874. By the late 1870s he had become a habitué of the Café de la Nouvelle-Athènes on the Place Pigalle in Montmartre, where he met and befriended Edgar Degas. The two artists, both difficult, ill-tempered characters, were to remain lifelong friends. Degas persuaded Zandomeneghi to exhibit at the fourth Impressionist exhibition in 1879, and the Italian also took part in the Impressionist exhibitions of 1880, 1881, and 1886.
While the artist's working habits and compositional choices link him to Degas and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, as well as Mary Cassatt and Berthe Morisot, his compositions are specific to him and his Italian heritage. Works like Young Woman with a Bouquet of Flowers earned him the additional nickname of “Le vénitien,” stemming from his brilliant yet subtle use of color that recalls the work of the Macchiaioli.

material: charcoal on paper
provenance:
Provenance:
L.G. Duke
Mathias Komor, New York
Sotheby's, New York, sale of January 29, 2010, lot 923.

Lot Essay:
A passionate draughtsman, Burne-Jones produced a large number of sketches and kept many of these in his studio until his death. The repetition of the study of the hand to the right of the present drawing suggests that it was likely intended as a working sketch, as does the inscription along the top edge, ‘Angel with King’ presumably a reference to the title or subject of the final composition.

While the gesture of a hand touching the face is a recurring motif in Burne-Jones’s paintings, the present work seems closer in spirit to the angel standing at the foot of King Arthur’s bed in The Sleep of King Arthur in Avalon, a colossal
painting now in Museo de Arte de Ponce, Puerto Rico, and considered to be the artist’s final masterpiece on which he worked for twenty years. Central to the composition, near the end of the bed, is a female figure standing next to a column. The figure appears in reverse in the present drawing; however, she holds her hand to her mouth in the gesture of silence, and has the same quality of stillness.

In comparison to the precise, highly refined drawings of the 1870s, in this late period, Burne-Jones’s drawing technique becomes softer, the chalk is more broadly swept, and stumping is used for areas of modeling. Further elegant, columnar figures, similar to this almost ethereal angel, inhabit other of the artist's last works. The writer Henry James described these works as "pictured abstraction."
